title: Your Gujarati Customers Know When You're Reading From a Translated Script

author: Ayush Kulkarni

body.text: Let Me Tell You a Story

body.html: Let me tell you about Rajesh. He runs an insurance agency in Coimbatore. His customers speak Tamil at home, English at the office, and a fluid mix of both when discussing premiums and policy details.
Rajesh tried one of those 'multilingual' voice platforms. The demo looked great. But when his customer said 'Enaku ₹5 lakh coverage venum, but EMI ethana varum?' — the system froze.
Why? Because it was trained on textbook Tamil and textbook English. Not the Tamil-English that 80 million Indians actually speak every day.
Code-switching isn't a bug in Indian speech. It's the feature. And most voice platforms treat it like an afterthought.
My uncle runs a pharmacy in Bengaluru. His customers speak Kannada at home, English at work, and a beautiful mix of both at his shop. No translation app captures that. No textbook teaches it.
Yet every 'multilingual' voice platform claims they 'support' Kannada.
Most people think voice AI 'speaks' languages. That's only half true. The real magic is in understanding — and understanding Indian speech is genuinely hard.

Indian speech isn't 'pure' language. A customer might say: 'Mujhe ₹5 lakh ka loan chahiye, EMI kitna hoga 3 years ke liye?' That's Hindi + English in one sentence. A 'multilingual' system that switches languages sentence-by-sentence can't handle this. It needs to understand both simultaneously.
Regional accents vary massively. Chennai Tamil isn't Madurai Tamil. Mumbai Hindi isn't Lucknow Hindi. A system trained on one accent fails on the other.
Speakers don't follow scripts. Your customer might interrupt, change topics, ask unexpected questions, or go silent while thinking. The AI needs to handle all of this naturally.

What Speaksy does differently: It's trained on real Indian phone conversations — not textbook language, not translated scripts. It understands Hinglish, Tanglish, Tenglish, Kanglish, Marathi-English, and Indian English as they are actually spoken. With code-switching handled naturally, not as an afterthought.
The result? Your customer feels like they're talking to someone who gets them. Not a robot reading from a translated sheet.

body.text: What This Actually Means for Your Business

body.html: What does 'understanding Indian languages' actually mean for your business?
It means your Tamil-speaking customer in Coimbatore doesn't have to switch to broken English to ask about their order.
It means your Kannada-speaking patient in Bengaluru can explain symptoms the way they actually talk — mixing English medical terms with Kannada descriptions — and be understood.
It means your Hindi-speaking insurance policyholder in Lucknow can ask 'Mera claim kitne din mein aa jayega?' and get a clear answer in the same language mix they used.

This isn't about checking a 'multilingual' box on a feature list. It's about the 250 million Indians who code-switch daily — who think in one language, count in another, and express emotions in a third. A voice platform that doesn't get that isn't built for India. It's built for a PowerPoint.
A major D2C brand launched in Tamil Nadu. Their voice support was 'English with Tamil option.'

Result? 68% of Tamil-speaking customers abandoned calls within 60 seconds. They couldn't navigate the English menus. The 'Tamil' option was formal, textbook Tamil — not the Tanglish their customers actually spoke.
After switching to a platform that understands real Tanglish:

items: Call abandonment dropped from 68% to 12%
Average call duration increased (customers stayed to complete their query)
CSAT scores for Tamil calls went from 2.8/5 to 4.3/5

body.html: One customer actually said: 'Finally, someone who speaks like me.'
That 'someone' was an AI. But the customer didn't care. They just wanted to be understood.

We didn't set out to build 'AI.' We set out to fix the phone call. Everything else followed.

author: Subhranshu Choudry

body.text: What This Actually Means for Your Business

body.html: What does smart outbound calling mean?
It means calling the right person at the right time with the right message.
Not calling 10,000 people and hoping 50 respond. Calling the 500 people who actually need to hear from you — based on their purchase history, their service due date, their behavior.
It means your 'outbound' calls feel like check-ins, not sales pitches. Like the car service center that called me because they knew my service was due.
Outbound isn't dead. Bad outbound is dead. The kind that interrupts dinner to sell credit cards. Smart outbound — relevant, timely, helpful — that's very much alive.
Your sales team dreads outbound calling. They procrastinate. They make 20 calls instead of 100. They hear 'not interested' 19 times and lose all enthusiasm.
What if outbound calls felt less like cold calling and more like checking in on someone who actually wanted to hear from you?

body.text: Let Me Tell You a Story

body.html: I hate receiving cold calls. You probably do too.

But last month, I got a call that didn't feel cold at all. It was from my car service center. The agent (AI or human, I couldn't tell) said: 'Mr. Choudry, your last service was 8 months ago. Your car has crossed 10,000 km. We have a slot this Saturday. Should I book it?'
I said yes. Because it was relevant. It was timely. It felt like someone was paying attention.
That's the difference between outbound calling and outbound caring. One annoys people. The other helps them.
Bad outbound: Call 10,000 people. Read a script. Hope 50 say yes. Annoy 9,950.
Smart outbound: Call the 500 people who actually need to hear from you. Have a conversation. Help them.
How it works:
1. Intelligence, not lists. The AI knows who's due for service, who abandoned a cart, who hasn't reordered consumables. It calls with purpose.
2. Timing matters. Calls at 11 AM on a Tuesday, not 8 PM during dinner. Respects DND. Follows regulatory hours.
3. Language matches the customer. Hinglish for Delhi, Tamil-English for Chennai, Kannada-English for Bengaluru. Not a one-size-fits-all script.
4. Conversation, not pitch. 'Hi Mr. Sharma, aapki car service 8 months overdue ho gayi hai. Saturday ka slot available hai. Book karun?' That's helpful. Not annoying.

5. Interested only. The AI qualifies interest. Only 'warm' leads — people who asked questions, showed interest, requested callback — get handed to your sales team. Your humans talk to interested prospects. Not cold names.
The result: 5x better response rates. Happier customers. And a sales team that actually enjoys their calls — because they're talking to people who want to talk back.
An automobile service chain. 40 centers across South India. Service reminders: manual calls by center staff. 200 calls per center monthly. 60% went unanswered.
After AI outbound:

items: AI calls: 8,000 monthly across all centers
Answer rate: 40% → 72% (better timing, local language)
Service bookings from calls: 35% → 58%
Revenue from reminder calls: ₹12 lakh monthly increase

Ask something not in the FAQ. 'What if I miss my EMI because my salary got delayed?' A knowledge-grounded agent will answer based on your actual policies. A prompt-dependent agent will hallucinate.

Call once. Ask something. Hang up. Call again from the same number. Ask a follow-up. Does the agent remember?
Test 5 — The Non-Tech Test
Give the login to your receptionist. Ask her to change the greeting. If she can't do it without calling IT, the platform isn't built for business users.
Pass all five? You have a real platform. Fail even one? Keep looking.

It means your Tamil-speaking customer in Coimbatore doesn't have to switch to broken English to ask about their order.

Speakers don't follow scripts. Your customer might interrupt, change topics, ask unexpected questions, or go silent while thinking. The AI needs to handle all of this naturally.

body.text: Let Me Tell You a Story

body.html: Last month, I sat through 6 voice AI demos from different platforms. Every single one started with a polished recording of an AI agent handling a perfect conversation.
So I asked each vendor the same thing: 'Can I call your demo number right now and interrupt the agent mid-sentence?'
Three said no — their demo was pre-recorded. Two said yes, and their agent broke. One said yes, and the agent adapted — paused, listened, and continued naturally.
That's the one I remembered. Because real customers don't follow scripts. They interrupt. They change topics. They get frustrated. Your voice AI needs to handle that.
When I evaluate voice AI platforms, I don't start with the demo. I start with one question: Can your agent handle my uncle interrupting mid-sentence?
Most can't. And that tells me everything I need to know.

body.text: What to Actually Test When Evaluating Voice AI

body.html: Don't trust demos. Trust your own test. Here's the 5-minute evaluation that separates real platforms from PowerPoint ones:
Test 1 — The Interruption Test
Call the demo number. Let the AI speak 3 sentences. Then interrupt. Change the topic. Ask something unrelated. A good agent adapts. A bad one breaks.
Test 2 — The Code-Switch Test
Speak in Hinglish. Mix Hindi and English in the same sentence. 'Mujhe ₹5 lakh ka health insurance chahiye, family ke liye, 2 bachche hain.' See if the agent understands naturally or gets confused.
Test 3 — The Edge Case Test
Ask something not in the FAQ. 'What if I miss my EMI because my salary got delayed?' A knowledge-grounded agent will answer based on your actual policies. A prompt-dependent agent will hallucinate.
Test 4 — The Memory Test
Call once. Ask something. Hang up. Call again from the same number. Ask a follow-up. Does the agent remember?
Test 5 — The Non-Tech Test
Give the login to your receptionist. Ask her to change the greeting. If she can't do it without calling IT, the platform isn't built for business users.
Pass all five? You have a real platform. Fail even one? Keep looking.

body.text: What This Actually Means for Your Business

body.html: What should you actually evaluate when choosing a voice AI platform?
Forget feature lists. Ask these five questions instead:

items: Can I test this on a real call right now? Not a demo. A real call to a real number.
What happens when my customer interrupts mid-sentence? This is the real test. Most platforms fail it.
Does it understand how my customers actually talk? Hinglish, Tanglish, code-switching — not textbook language.

It means your Tamil-speaking customer in Coimbatore doesn't have to switch to broken English to ask about their order.

Most people think voice AI 'speaks' languages. That's only half true. The real magic is in understanding — and understanding Indian speech is genuinely hard.

Indian speech isn't 'pure' language. A customer might say: 'Mujhe ₹5 lakh ka loan chahiye, EMI kitna hoga 3 years ke liye?' That's Hindi + English in one sentence. A 'multilingual' system that switches languages sentence-by-sentence can't handle this. It needs to understand both simultaneously.
Regional accents vary massively. Chennai Tamil isn't Madurai Tamil. Mumbai Hindi isn't Lucknow Hindi. A system trained on one accent fails on the other.
Speakers don't follow scripts. Your customer might interrupt, change topics, ask unexpected questions, or go silent while thinking. The AI needs to handle all of this naturally.

It understands Hinglish, Tanglish, Tenglish, Kanglish, Marathi-English, and Indian English as they are actually spoken. With code-switching handled naturally, not as an afterthought.
The result? Your customer feels like they're talking to someone who gets them. Not a robot reading from a translated sheet.

title: Five Questions Your Voice AI Vendor Hopes You Never Ask
excerpt: Let Me Tell You a Story Last month, I sat through 6 voice AI demos from different platforms. Every single one started with a polished recording of an AI agent handling a perfect…
author: Ayush Kulkarni

body.text: Let Me Tell You a Story

body.html: Last month, I sat through 6 voice AI demos from different platforms. Every single one started with a polished recording of an AI agent handling a perfect conversation.
So I asked each vendor the same thing: 'Can I call your demo number right now and interrupt the agent mid-sentence?'
Three said no — their demo was pre-recorded. Two said yes, and their agent broke. One said yes, and the agent adapted — paused, listened, and continued naturally.
That's the one I remembered. Because real customers don't follow scripts. They interrupt. They change topics. They get frustrated. Your voice AI needs to handle that.
When I evaluate voice AI platforms, I don't start with the demo. I start with one question: Can your agent handle my uncle interrupting mid-sentence?
Most can't. And that tells me everything I need to know.

body.text: What to Actually Test When Evaluating Voice AI

body.html: Don't trust demos. Trust your own test. Here's the 5-minute evaluation that separates real platforms from PowerPoint ones:
Test 1 — The Interruption Test
Call the demo number. Let the AI speak 3 sentences. Then interrupt. Change the topic. Ask something unrelated. A good agent adapts. A bad one breaks.
Test 2 — The Code-Switch Test
Speak in Hinglish. Mix Hindi and English in the same sentence. 'Mujhe ₹5 lakh ka health insurance chahiye, family ke liye, 2 bachche hain.' See if the agent understands naturally or gets confused.
Test 3 — The Edge Case Test
Ask something not in the FAQ. 'What if I miss my EMI because my salary got delayed?' A knowledge-grounded agent will answer based on your actual policies. A prompt-dependent agent will hallucinate.
Test 4 — The Memory Test
Call once. Ask something. Hang up. Call again from the same number. Ask a follow-up. Does the agent remember?
Test 5 — The Non-Tech Test
Give the login to your receptionist. Ask her to change the greeting. If she can't do it without calling IT, the platform isn't built for business users.
Pass all five? You have a real platform. Fail even one? Keep looking.

body.text: What This Actually Means for Your Business

body.html: What should you actually evaluate when choosing a voice AI platform?
Forget feature lists. Ask these five questions instead:

items: Can I test this on a real call right now? Not a demo. A real call to a real number.
What happens when my customer interrupts mid-sentence? This is the real test. Most platforms fail it.
Does it understand how my customers actually talk? Hinglish, Tanglish, code-switching — not textbook language.
How long from signup to live? If it's more than a day for a basic setup, you're buying a project, not a product.
Can my non-technical team manage this? If you need a developer to change a greeting, it's not built for business users.

body.html: Everything else is marketing.

Case studies with Fortune 500 logos

Setup in hours, not months
Non-technical teams managing it independently

If the answer is yes, test it. If the answer depends on perfect performance, keep looking.
